style.vernacular: A city of contrasts: most residents live in communist-era prefabricated concrete apartment blocks (blocuri) of 4-11 storeys in grey and faded pastel render, many wrapped in coloured insulation; between them survive 19th-century neoclassical and eclectic 'Little Paris' townhouses and palaces in ochre, cream and white stucco, Brancovenesc and Neo-Romanian houses with tiled hip roofs and arcaded porches, and interwar Art Deco and modernist apartment blocks in cream stucco. Glass-and-steel offices and large retail boxes stand on the northern and eastern edges. Orthodox churches are small whitewashed or stuccoed buildings with tiled or metal domes and open porches; suburbs and Ilfov villages are low plastered houses with hip roofs.
style.ornament: Brancovenesc stone carving, stucco and arcaded loggias; neoclassical pediments and Corinthian pilasters (Stirbei Palace, former National Theatre, old University); Gothic Revival (House of Guilds 1859-62); Art Deco and interwar modernist balconies and corner windows; Arcul de Triumf and Palatul Telefoanelor; Ceausescu-era socialist-realist colonnades and the Palace of the Parliament.

sources.what: Brancovenesc (baroque with oriental features, stone carving, stucco), 19th-century neoclassical Bucharest (Stirbei Palace c.1835, National Theatre 1849-52, old University 1857-64), Wallachian Gothic Revival, interwar Art Deco/Modernism, communist socialist-realist demolitions
Paris of the East late 19th century; interwar Arcul de Triumf and Palatul Telefoanelor; most residents in communist-era high-density apartment blocks; Palace of the Parliament
